results.title: PyPIGuard: A Lightweight, Explainable Machine Learning Tool for Pre-Install Detection of Malicious PyPI Packages
results.abstract: Open-source package registries such as PyPI are increasingly targeted by at-tackers, yet existing detection tools report false-positive rates as high as 97%,making automated adoption impractical. PyPIGuard is an open-source, de-ployable tool that classifies PyPI packages as malicious or benign withina millisecond, using only static code, Abstract Syntax Tree (AST), andbytecode-level structural features — without relying on a large languagemodel (LLM). It is deployed as a live web application with a real-time scan-ner, a file-upload scanner, and a Jupyter notebook malware-import scanner.Trained on 9,723 real packages — the entire available malicious archive plusfreshly-sampled benign packages — it achieves 0.9993 ROC-AUC on held-outdata and 0.984 ROC-AUC on packages discovered after the training cutoff,remaining robust under adversarial evasion testing.

SecureFedIDS: Enhancing Federated Intrusion Detection in Smart Home IoT Networks through Malicious Update Detection and Blockchain Verification
results.abstract: The rapid proliferation of smart home Internet of Things (IoT) devices has introduced significant cybersecurity challenges, including unauthorized access, malicious traffic, data manipulation, and coordinated network attacks. Conventional intrusion detection systems often face limitations associated with centralized data processing, privacy exposure, computational constraints, and vulnerability to adversarial manipulation. Federated learning offers a privacy-preserving alternative by enabling distributed model training without requiring raw data to leave individual devices. However, malicious participants can exploit this collaborative architecture by submitting poisoned model updates that compromise detection accuracy and system reliability. This article proposes SecureFedIDS, a blockchain-enhanced federated intrusion detection framework designed to improve the integrity, reliability, and privacy of collaborative learning in smart home IoT networks. The framework integrates local intrusion detection, malicious update assessment, blockchain-based verification, reputation-aware participant selection, and secure model aggregation. Each participating device or gateway trains a local detection model using its own network traffic, while an update validation mechanism evaluates submitted parameters for suspicious deviations, anomalous gradients, and inconsistencies with expected learning behavior. Blockchain technology provides a tamper-evident record of validated updates, verification outcomes, and aggregation decisions, supporting traceability and accountability across distributed participants. The proposed architecture also incorporates resource-aware processing and privacyconscious information exchange to accommodate heterogeneous smart home environments. A structured evaluation framework is outlined to assess detection performance, poisoning resilience, communication overhead, computational efficiency, and privacy-related risks against conventional federated and centralized baselines. Rather than assuming unmeasured improvements, the framework establishes measurable criteria for determining whether SecureFedIDS can deliver reliable intrusion detection under adversarial conditions. The proposed approach provides a foundation for trustworthy, decentralized, and resilient cybersecurity in interconnected smart homes while identifying implementation challenges associated with blockchain scalability, adaptive attacks, device heterogeneity, and secure model coordination.

results.title: Three-Electrode Electrochemical Cell Setup and Pre-Measurement Check v1
results.abstract: This protocol provides a practical pre-measurement checklist for assembling and validating a three-electrode electrochemical cell. It covers electrode inspection, positioning, lead verification, electrolyte handling, bubble removal, open-circuit stabilization, and conservative first measurements to reduce setup-related artifacts.

results.title: Use of runtime verification for audit trail check in remote verification of measuring instruments
results.abstract: Abstract In legal metrology, the reliability of individual measuring instruments is confirmed through verification in the form of compliance with requirements. Recently, remote verification has gained attention as a means to perform verification without on-site visits by verification officers. A key concern of remote verification is ensuring that the instrument has not been subject to unauthorized interventions during its use. The record of legally relevant events of a measuring instrument provides a way to address this concern; such a record is called an audit trail, and checking an audit trail enables the detection of unauthorized interventions. Since a manual check of an audit trail is time-consuming and impractical, the previous studies proposed using runtime verification (RV), aiming to automate audit trail checks. However, the previous studies do not consider the requirements related to remote verification, leaving a gap in their applicability to remote verification. In the present study, we demonstrated the audit trail check using RV under conditions reflecting the requirements related to remote verification, by evaluating audit trails generated from assumed operational scenarios. Through the demonstration, we obtained events and formal descriptions, which may contribute to the implementation of remote verification of measuring instruments. Moreover, this contribution may also be applicable to confirming compliance with specific requirements in measuring instruments outside the scope of legal metrology.

Adaptive Testing with Costly Verification and Pre-Test Communication
results.abstract: I study adaptive testing when a principal bears the cost of verification and a privately informed agent can exert unobservable effort to affect test outcomes. With costly tests, performance determines both what the principal learns and which future verification path the agent receives. Consequently, without pre-test communication, restricting attention to mechanisms that induce full effort can be strictly costly: strategic shirking can be valuable for routing types across verification paths. Pre-test communication eliminates the need for such performancebased routing. When the agent selects among committed tracks before testing, full effort is without loss on the truthfully assigned track, and communication weakly dominates no-communication mechanisms, including those that exploit strategic shirking. The key construction replaces the bottom type's testing procedure with a no-test lottery that preserves his hiring probability. I characterize the optimal communication mechanism: the bottom-type track is test-free, while the remaining high-type track solves a finite linear program and may require randomization. With many types, the same logic isolates a test-free bottom track; with a continuum, it generates a shrinking bottom pool whose value gain is second order in testing costs.

Modelstamp: Pre-Deserialization Verification of Machine-Learning Artifacts and Runtime Environment State
results.abstract: Persisted machine-learning models can remain byte-identical while the software environments in which they are loaded evolve, creating a verification problem that artifact integrity checks alone cannot expose. This paper presents Modelstamp, a lightweight Python persistence library for verifying artifact integrity and represented runtime-environment state before deserialization. At persistence time, Modelstamp associates a serialized artifact with a sidecar JSON manifest containing a SHA-256 digest, runtime metadata, and installed versions from a bounded tracked-package set; a separately recorded model-relevant subset determines which package versions participate in drift comparison. Optional HMAC authentication supports workflows in which the producer and verifier share a secret key. At verification time, the artifact and represented current environment are checked against this recorded evidence before the model is deserialized. Modelstamp is evaluated using 14 controlled environment-drift scenarios, eight controlled trust-boundary scenarios, and an artifact-size scaling benchmark from 10 MiB to 1 GiB. The controlled drift experiments behaved as specified across relevant dependency changes, unchanged environments, and unrelated environmental changes, including broader noise controls. The trust-boundary experiments similarly confirmed both intended detections and expected limitations, including shared-key forgery and replay. Median verification time increased from 0.032 s at 10 MiB to 3.334 s at 1 GiB, with measured throughput of approximately 307-312 MiB/s in the benchmark environment. These results characterize Modelstamp as a complementary pre-deserialization reference-state verification control rather than as a replacement for dependency-management systems, malicious-model detection, safe deserialization, or public publisher authentication.
